payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a root epic with open children and an unapproved decompose checkpoint when loop preflight runs then it refuses the verdict and names the approval command and distinguishes a checkpoint a live grant can auto-resolve from one it cannot serve
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run basicly loop preflight basicly-yc0x     # VERDICT: ready
uv run basicly loop supervise basicly-yc0x --autonomy L3
```

Observed 2026-08-04 - `preflight` printed **`VERDICT: ready`** with a clean base, a live L3 grant, a
funded forecast and five in-band lanes. `supervise` then dispatched **nothing**:

```
routed:   basicly-yc0x -> seed-blocked - no lane could be provisioned from 5 open
          child(ren) - decompose checkpoint awaiting human approval
blocked:  no ready lanes and nothing to land
```

Expected - a command whose stated job is "check everything a supervised run needs before it starts"
does not report ready for a run that cannot dispatch a single lane.

## Context

The epic's own `decompose` checkpoint is a human gate and **a covering grant cannot serve it** - an
L3 grant on the root does not approve the root's own decomposition. That is correct behaviour. The
defect is that `preflight` does not look at it, so its verdict is false precisely where an operator
most needs it: before spending the wall-clock of a fan-out that will refuse.

This is the promise `basicly-ze8z` exists to keep - if you need to remember a precondition,
`preflight` is wrong rather than the operator. It already checks the clean base, live worktrees,
stale bindings, the resolved runner, the grant, the budget, dispatchable-versus-seedable counts, the
per-lane cost and the pass bound. The checkpoint state is the one precondition it omits, and it is
the one that cost a refused pass this session.

Cheap to detect: `policy` already reconstructs checkpoint state for `loop status`, which reported
`checkpoints: (none)` on the epic at the same moment.

## Fix shape

- `preflight` reports the root's own unapproved checkpoints and **refuses the verdict** when one of
  them blocks provisioning, naming the exact approval command - the same shape it already uses for
  the missing-budget blocker.
- Distinguish a checkpoint a live grant *will* auto-resolve from one it cannot serve. Reporting every
  unapproved checkpoint as a blocker would make the verdict noise; the useful line is "this one needs
  a human because a covering grant cannot serve its own root".
- Regression test proven red first (`basicly-kjc5.49`): an epic with open children and an unapproved
  `decompose` checkpoint must not preflight as ready.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_cli.py`
payload.title: Preflight reports ready for a pass the decompose checkpoint will refuse

payload.text:
A cheaper reproduction, measured 2026-08-05 at d31f6bd. The bead's case needs an unapproved decompose checkpoint; this one needs nothing but the epic's current state:

  uv run basicly loop preflight basicly-yc0x
  base:      clean
  grant:     L3, spent 53408271 under it, remaining 96591729
  lanes:     0 dispatchable now, 0 open child(ren)
  forecast:  ~82595185 tokens if all 5 lanes start (cap x per-lane)
  VERDICT:   ready

Every child of basicly-yc0x closed on 2026-08-04, so there is no lane to provision and no checkpoint involved at all - yet the verdict is 'ready'. This is the bead's own Expected line ('a command whose stated job is to check everything a supervised run needs does not report ready for a run that cannot dispatch a single lane') reached by a shorter path than the checkpoint.

Two consequences for the fix:

1. The refusal predicate is 'zero dispatchable lanes', of which the unapproved checkpoint is one cause and an all-closed child set is another. Fixing only the checkpoint case leaves this one green, so write the predicate on the dispatchable count and report the cause.
2. The forecast line is incoherent with the lane line in the same output - it prices 5 lanes while the line above says 0 open children, because it multiplies the concurrency cap by the per-lane figure without reference to what exists. A reader sizing a pass from that number sizes a pass that cannot run. Worth a regression assertion that the forecast never prices more lanes than there are dispatchable children.

Correction to the previous comment, same day, before any lane builds against it.

That comment proposed writing the refusal predicate on 'zero dispatchable lanes'. **That predicate is wrong and would refuse every legitimate pass.** The harness-loop runbook states it directly: 'lanes: 0 dispatchable now counts *adopted* lanes. Before any worktree exists it reads zero and that is not a blocker - the supervisor provisions from the ranked open children at pass start.' Verified here - with two open children both sized 'in band', preflight still prints '0 dispatchable now' and the pass is genuinely ready.

What the reproduction actually shows is narrower and still real: preflight printed VERDICT ready when basicly-yc0x had **0 open children**, so there was nothing to provision from. The distinguishing signal is the open-child set and the band table, not the dispatchable count:

- refuse when there are **no open children at all** (nothing to provision), and
- refuse when every open child is 'REFUSED - too large, split it' (children exist but none can dispatch).

Also verified: the epic's decompose checkpoint reports APPROVED here, so the checkpoint case in the bead body is a *third* distinct cause rather than the same one. Three causes, one verdict line - which is the argument for reporting the cause rather than just flipping the verdict.

The forecast observation in the previous comment stands unchanged: the line prices 5 lanes (cap x per-lane) while the line above says 0 open children, and it did so again at 2 open children. It is not referenced to what exists.

1. Note package.json has no "name" key.

payload.description:
## Context

Second refusal of the v0.10.0 release on 2026-08-28, reproduced in a scratch clone by applying the release steps and running `.basicly/core/hooks/pre-commit.py` over the staged tree: the hook exited 0 and rewrote `docs/architecture/architecture.md`. The pre-commit framework fails a hook that modifies a file, so the release commit was refused and the routed text carried no check name.

The version bump `0.9.0` to `0.10.0` adds one character to the header of every projected instruction file, and `docs/architecture/architecture.md` carries the `always-on-sizes` generated block that states those sizes to the character. `release._regenerate` runs `basicly build` so the projections carry the new version, and nothing regenerates the docs-claims blocks that describe the projections, so the release commit is stale on arrival at its own gate.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Clone this repo at d7860cf4, `uv sync --group dev`, copy `node_modules`.
2. In Python: `release.plan_release`, then `_bump_version_file`, `_regenerate`, `_rewrite_pins`, `_assemble_fragments`, `_write_changelog`; `git add -A`.
3. `uv run python .basicly/core/hooks/pre-commit.py`; exit 0; `git status` shows `docs/architecture/architecture.md` modified by 3 lines of the always-on-sizes table.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN `release._regenerate` runs, IT SHALL also run the `docs-claims` check's declared `fix_command` from `basicly.toml`, so every generated block that describes the projections is current in the release commit.
- WHEN the repository declares no `docs-claims` check, `_regenerate` SHALL run the projection rebuild alone and refuse nothing.
- WHEN a regression test applies a release to a fixture whose `docs-claims` fix command writes a marker file, IT SHALL assert the marker exists after `_regenerate` and that the release commit contains no unstaged change.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/release.py`
- `tests/test_release_assembly.py`
- `changelog.d/<this-id>.fixed.md`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: the reproduction above ends with `git status --short` empty after the hook, and the real `basicly release 0.10.0` commit passes `pre-commit-script`.

payload.description:
## Context

Session 2026-08-14. The handover carried the trap in plain words - "measure headroom before writing
prose, not after a gate refuses you" - and it was still paid for **three times in one session**,
because there are two ratchets and measuring one feels like having measured.

Each time, `module-size` headroom was measured and `comment-density` was not:

```text
basicly-jn1x   runner.py 59.9% vs frozen 59.8, run_record.py 58.0% vs 56.9
               two rounds of prose-trimming after the gate refused
basicly-c357   differential.py had +3 tokens AND 0.0pt density; the placement
               had to be redesigned into a new kit module
basicly-ejdm.2 lane_split.py landed at 56.5% against a 50% cap on a new file
```

The module-size trap is the one this repo has written down most, which is probably why it is the
one that gets measured.

## The shape of the fix

One command that takes a path and reports **both** ratchets in one answer - tokens against the
frozen baseline or cap, and prose share against the frozen share or cap - so "measure headroom"
is a single call rather than two an agent will half-do. `check_module_size.tracked_modules` and
`check_comment_density.tracked_modules` already produce both halves; nothing composes them.

Neither script currently takes a path argument either, so today the measurement is a python
one-liner importing both from `.scripts/`, which is why it is skipped under time pressure.

## What this is not

Not a new gate. Both ratchets already bind at commit time. This is the read that lets a change be
sized before it is written, which is the only point at which the information is cheap.
payload.title: measuring ratchet headroom takes two commands so an agent measures one and pays for the other

basicly-ejdm.2 lane_split.py landed at 56.5% against a 50% cap on a new file

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-08-20 while refuting `basicly-mbkqxi`, and deliberately **not** claimed as that
record's cause.

`tracker.scrub_ledger` is the only writer in the tree that rewrites the owned ledger **whole**
- `read_text`, write a temp file, rename - and it takes **no `LedgerLock`**. Every other writer
goes through `events.append`, which holds the lock for the duration of one append. So anything
appended between this function's read and its rename is destroyed, and destroyed silently: the
rename succeeds, the log parses, and the fold is internally consistent because the lost lines
were never in the text that was re-emitted.

**Why this is filed as a hazard and not as `basicly-mbkqxi`'s cause.** It re-emits every line
it read, so it cannot produce a *single interior* deletion, which is the shape `basicly-vkh0.30`
shows. It can only truncate a suffix of concurrent appends. The cause of that hole remains
unidentified.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read `src/basicly/tracker.py:800` and observe the read-modify-rename sequence.
2. Search that function for `LedgerLock` and observe none, against a positive control that finds the lock in `events.append`.
3. Observe `events.append` takes the lock for the duration of one append, so the two writers do not exclude each other.
4. Observe that a line appended after the `read_text` and before the rename is absent from the temp file and therefore absent after it.
5. Observe the result parses cleanly and folds consistently, so no gate reports it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a whole-file ledger rewrite when it runs then it holds the same lock an append holds, so the two cannot interleave - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_tracker_scrub_ledger.py -k lock -q`
- Given an append that arrives during a rewrite then it is either serialised behind it or refused, never dropped
- Given the lock is held then the hold is bounded, because a rewrite reads the whole log and an append that waited forever would be worse than one that failed

## Scope

- `src/basicly/tracker.py`
- `tests/test_tracker_scrub_ledger.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/tracker.py`
- `tests/test_tracker_scrub_ledger.py`
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_tracker_scrub_ledger.py -q`

## Context

Surfaced while verifying the codex capability facts for basicly-lelg (2026-07-31, against the live
OpenAI docs). Not a defect — an unexamined opportunity, and a policy comment that may now be narrower
than it reads.

`src/basicly/agents.py:23-25` renders every subagent to `.claude/agents/<slug>.md` **only**, and the
comment gives the reason as "Single output root (basicly-2f4 policy): Claude Code reads only
.claude/agents". That statement is true *about Claude*, but it is not a statement about codex, and it
reads today as though the single root were settled for every agent family.

OpenAI now documents a repo-checked-in subagent surface: "add standalone TOML files under
`~/.codex/agents/` for personal agents or `.codex/agents/` for project-scoped agents", each defining
`name`, `description`, and `developer_instructions`. So there is a real second target for the subagent
tier that basicly does not project to.

Worth deciding rather than assuming, because the roster work (basicly-s2xf, v0.9.0) is where the
subagent tier gets its real content, and doubling the surface after that lands is more expensive than
deciding now.

Points the decision has to weigh:

- The format differs: our subagents render as markdown with frontmatter for Claude; codex wants TOML
  with a fixed field set. That is a new renderer and a new drift gate, not a second path in the same
  template.
- `agents-check` would need the same `--all-default-roots` treatment `skills-check` has, or it will
  pass while the codex root drifts (the failure mode basicly recorded for `.agents/`).
- Read the `2f4` decision first and check whether codex was considered and rejected, or simply not yet
  in scope. If it was a deliberate reject, close this and record the reason next to the comment so the
  next reader does not re-open it.
- No always-on cost either way: subagents are on-demand files, so this does not touch the AGENTS.md
  headroom problem.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the 2f4 single-root policy and the documented codex project agents surface when this is decided then either subagents project to the codex root with a renderer and a drift gate covering it, or the decision to stay Claude-only is recorded with its reason beside the AGENTS_OUTPUT_ROOT comment so it is not re-opened

payload.description:
## The defect

basicly-vkh0.45 moved the per-work-type required sections into `[policy.type_sections]` in `basicly.toml`. It moved the **reader** that judges a record, not the **writer** that scaffolds one.

`policy.compose_body` and `policy.scaffold_body` hold no repository root, so they cannot reach the configuration. Their two callers — `decompose._child_body` and `cli._cmd_policy_scaffold` — were outside that record's scope fence, and the lane deliberately declined to add a `repo_root` parameter nothing passed.

The result is a split brain. A repository that declares `bug = ["## Repro Steps"]` gets a Definition-of-Ready that demands that heading, and a `basicly policy scaffold --type bug` that emits the built-in one instead. The scaffold's own output then fails the gate the scaffold exists to satisfy, and the failure message points the user back at the same command.

A second, smaller half: `policy._SECTION_HINTS` is keyed on the two built-in headings, so a configured heading scaffolds the generic `TODO: fill this in.` placeholder rather than a tailored hint.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In `basicly.toml`, set `[policy.type_sections]` `bug = ["## Repro Steps", "## Impact"]`.
2. `uv run basicly policy scaffold --type bug` — read the headings it emits.
3. Create a record from exactly that scaffold output.
4. `uv run basicly policy dor <id>` on it.

Observed: step 2 emits the built-in headings. Step 4 reports NOT READY, missing the two configured ones, and advises running the command from step 2.
Expected: the scaffold emits the headings the configured rule requires, so its output passes Definition-of-Ready by construction.

## Acceptance Criteria

Given a repository that declares `[policy.type_sections]`, when `basicly policy scaffold --type <t>` runs, then it emits exactly the headings that work type's configured rule requires.
Given the scaffold's own output, when it is used as a record body unchanged, then `basicly policy dor` reports the section requirement satisfied, so the two halves cannot disagree.
Given a decomposed child body from `decompose._child_body`, then it is built from the same configured set.
Given a configured heading with no entry in the section hints, then the placeholder names the heading rather than printing a bare generic line.
Given no configuration, then the built-in set is scaffolded exactly as today.
Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_policy.py tests/test_decompose.py -k scaffold -q

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_policy.py`

payload.description:
## Context

**Corrected 2026-07-30 after the owner sharpened the criterion.** The first version of this epic
read the directive as "zero runtime dependencies" and set out to remove `jinja2`, `jsonschema`,
`pyyaml`, `rich`, `uv`, the pre-commit framework and node. That was wrong, and the correction
matters because it removes a large breaking change from the roadmap.

The axis is not external-versus-internal, nor binary-versus-package. It is:

> **Can we absorb this component's breaking change on our own schedule, or does it dictate terms
> to us?**

A **library or framework** is fine. It is versioned, we pin it, and when it ships a breaking
change we upgrade when ready and fix our own code. The blast radius is our source.

A **product** is not. `beads` is the case in point, and the evidence is already recorded in
`docs/design/work-tracker.md` section 2.10: crossing one of its schema migrations requires
*"exactly one designated clone"* to run `bd migrate` and `bd dolt push` while every other clone
installs the new binary and runs `bd bootstrap`. That is a coordinated, human-sequenced,
multi-machine operation sitting in our critical path. Worse, the upgrade is sometimes not
available at all: br's current main targets schema 17 and its reviewed migration accepts only
13-to-17 and 14-to-17, so a 0.2.19 database has no supported path forward from schema 16. A
dependency we cannot upgrade, and cannot decline to upgrade, is not a dependency we manage.

The compounding factor is that beads owns **our state** - every phase derivation, gate,
checkpoint, dependency edge, decision and run record. A library that owns no state can be swapped
in an afternoon; a product that owns the state cannot be swapped at all without a migration.

## The rule

**No third-party product may own basicly's state.** Libraries and frameworks are permitted and
pinned. An optional extension - existing skills, language or technology guidelines - is permitted
and must stay optional.

## Classification of every current dependency

| Component | Class | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jinja2`, `jsonschema`, `pyyaml`, `ruamel.yaml`, `rich` | library | **Keep.** Pinned, semver, owns no state. The catalog stays YAML - the stdlib-has-no-YAML-parser problem is no longer forcing a move to TOML. |
| `uv` | tool | **Keep.** Versioned, replaceable, owns no state. |
| pre-commit framework | framework | **Keep.** Dispatches our hooks; owns no state. |
| node (markdownlint hook) | tool | **Keep**, but it is the weakest entry - it is the only one whose absence has actually broken a commit path on this machine, and it earns a re-examination on its own merits rather than under this rule. |
| Python 3.14+ | language runtime | **Keep.** Not a product. Whether the floor should drop is an adoption question, not this one. |
| **`br` / beads** | **product that owns our state** | **Remove.** This is the whole of the directive. Tracked by `basicly-vkh0`. |
| **`bv`** | **product** | **Remove.** Measured at 0 of 141 surfaces used (`basicly-vkh0.2`), so this is a deletion rather than a replacement. |

## Why this epic still exists rather than folding into vkh0

`vkh0` removes the one product we have. This epic is the **policy** that stops the next one
arriving, which is the part that outlives the migration: the rule above written down where an
agent proposing a dependency will read it, the classification kept current, and a gate that
refuses a new runtime dependency it cannot classify.

## Success Criteria

- The dependency rule is stated in the architecture reference, every current dependency is classified against it, `br` and `bv` are gone from the runtime path, and a check refuses a newly added runtime dependency that is not classifiable as a library or framework

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the harness after this epic closes when the full loop is driven in a consumer repo then no third-party product is invoked or required, the permitted libraries are pinned and declared, and a gate fails when a new runtime dependency is introduced without a recorded classification

payload.text: OWNER CLARIFICATION 2026-08-13: br and bv are NOT removed from the system - other projects use them. The goal is that no project vendoring basicly HAS to use them, and that basicly itself stops using br once the work tracker is fully implemented. So this epic is about removing the *dependency*, not the *support*: br stays a usable store for a consumer that wants it, and bv is not deleted. Any disposition in this bead reading 'Remove - this is a deletion rather than a replacement' for bv is superseded by this note.

in an afternoon; a product that owns the state cannot be swapped at all without a migration.

## The rule

**No third-party product may own basicly's state.** Libraries and frameworks are permitted and
pinned. An optional extension - existing skills, language or technology guidelines - is permitted
and must stay optional.

## Classification of every current dependency

| Component | Class | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jinja2`, `jsonschema`, `pyyaml`, `ruamel.yaml`, `rich` | library | **Keep.** Pinned, semver, owns no state. The catalog stays YAML - the stdlib-has-no-YAML-parser problem is no longer forcing a move to TOML. |
| `uv` | tool | **Keep.** Versioned, replaceable, owns no state. |
| pre-commit framework | framework | **Keep.** Dispatches our hooks; owns no state. |
| node (markdownlint hook) | tool | **Keep**, but it is the weakest entry - it is the only one whose absence has actually broken a commit path on this machine, and it earns a re-examination on its own merits rather than under this rule. |
| Python 3.14+ | language runtime | **Keep.** Not a product. Whether the floor should drop is an adoption question, not this one. |
| **`br` / beads** | **product that owns our state** | **Remove.** This is the whole of the directive. Tracked by `basicly-vkh0`. |
| **`bv`** | **product** | **Remove.** Measured at 0 of 141 surfaces used (`basicly-vkh0.2`), so this is a deletion rather than a replacement. |

## Why this epic still exists rather than folding into vkh0

`vkh0` removes the one product we have. This epic is the **policy** that stops the next one
arriving, which is the part that outlives the migration: the rule above written down where an
agent proposing a dependency will read it, the classification kept current, and a gate that
refuses a new runtime dependency it cannot classify.

## Success Criteria

- The dependency rule is stated in the architecture reference, every current dependency is classified against it, `br` and `bv` are gone from the runtime path, and a check refuses a newly added runtime dependency that is not classifiable as a library or framework

- `src/basicly/claude_settings.py`
- their tests

       rg -n '^append_only_paths' basicly.toml

   Observed 2026-08-19: `append_only_paths = []`, and `append_only_report` returns its
   "no append-only path declared" line for an empty list before it reaches the membership
   test. So the reproduction belongs in `tests/test_contention.py` against a fixture repo
   that configures `append_only_paths = ["CHANGELOG.md"]`, not against this checkout.
3. In that fixture, give two lanes a `## Scope`: one declaring the glob `*.md` on its own
   backticked line, one declaring nothing that covers `CHANGELOG.md`. Call
   `contention.append_only_report` with both lanes.

declares it` line, so the report names a lane that did declare it and the operator reads a
`contend:` line that is false.

same glob test the landing uses. The function's own docstring already states that intent -
"A lane that *declares* the path in its own `## Scope` is left out of the count" - so this is
the docstring's rule failing on a glob, not a behaviour change.

## Context

`basicly-u2hl.54.1` made `validate-as-consumer` a required gate for a unit whose recorded
`[harness-classification]` marker names L3. The augmentation is applied at
`loop_state.read_node_state` and at `cli._cmd_policy_gate`, so the derived phase and
`basicly policy gate` both answer against the unit own required set.

`policy._ship_delegation_violations` (`policy.py:2264`) is the third caller of
`policy.gate_status` and was deliberately left on the base config, because that function
is the L3 ship-delegation refusal rather than the loop own ladder, and `policy.py` sits at
**10 tokens of headroom** under the module-size ratchet (32,472 of a frozen 32,482), so
the change could not be made there without an extraction.

Consequence: under an L3 autonomy grant, `_ship_delegation_violations` reads
`can_advance` over `("verify",)` only, so a unit resting in VALIDATE does not appear as a
violation. It is not exploitable today - the loop own `_on_ship` is unreachable while the
gate is outstanding, because `derive_phase` returns `validate` rather than `ship` - so this
is a missing second layer, not an open door.

payload.description:
## Context

`basicly loop advance <id>` at the build to verify boundary briefs a repair and dispatches a
metered `claude -p` implementer when the landing gate failed. It does this without checking
whether a grant with remaining budget covers the dispatch.

Observed 2026-08-13 on `basicly-ef7t`. The L3 grant on `basicly-u2hl` was already spent
(315,547,342 of 300,000,000) and a decision saying so was sitting in the queue
(`basicly-u2hl#201ea56f76`, "the session is human-only until re-granted"). The advance
briefed and spawned the repair agent anyway. It ran for over 10 minutes and had written
nothing when it was killed; the spend is unmeasured because the run recorded no entry.

`--runner manual` is the workaround and it works, but it has to be remembered per
invocation.

Related but not the same defect: `basicly-rupz` covers the ceiling not stopping a dispatch
already started. This one is about never starting it.

## Proposed check

A test that puts a spent grant on the root, drives a unit to a failed landing gate, runs the
advance, and asserts no runner subprocess is spawned and the escalation names the missing
budget instead.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Have a spent grant on the root, with the decision already queued saying so - observed
   2026-08-13, `basicly-u2hl#201ea56f76`: "L3 grant token_budget spent (315547342/300000000
   tokens under this grant); the session is human-only until re-granted".
2. Drive a unit to a failed landing gate, then run the advance:

   ```sh
   uv run basicly loop advance <issue>
   ```

3. Observed on `basicly-ef7t`: the first advance reported
   `[blocked] build -> build: merge failed: verify full failed: pytest (rework 1/2); briefed a
   repair for gate 'merge'`, and the **second** advance spawned
   `claude --agent implementer --model claude-opus-5 -p ...` as a subprocess. It ran for over ten
   minutes, had written nothing when it was killed, and the spend is **unmeasured** because the
   run recorded no entry.
4. `--runner manual` prevents it, which is the workaround, not the fix: it has to be remembered
   per invocation and nothing warns when it is forgotten.

Distinct from `basicly-rupz` (closed), which covered a ceiling not stopping a dispatch already
started. This is about never starting one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a root whose grant has no remaining token budget, when an advance would brief and
  dispatch a metered repair, then no runner subprocess is spawned - check: a test puts a spent
  grant on the root, drives a failed landing gate, runs the advance, and asserts the runner was
  never invoked.

payload.description:
The commit-msg hook (.basicly/core/hooks/commit-msg.py) rejects any commit whose description contains characters outside [a-z0-9 space hyphen] — no capitals, no periods/dots. This is a stricter-than-spec house profile: Conventional Commits v1.0.0 itself places NO charset restriction on the description and its body is free-form (verified against the spec). The conventional-commits skill already documents lowercase-only and 'reword version strings', but it tells agents to REWORD out dotted/uppercase forms rather than move them to the free-form body, and it lacks the two real-rejection examples. The hook's error is also generic (does not name the offending character). Two real rejections in one session: 'Font Awesome v4' (capitals) and 'restamp the install to 0.2.0' (the dots in a version number).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Attempt a commit with a capitalized proper noun (e.g. 'feat: add Font Awesome v4 icons') or a dotted version (e.g. 'chore: restamp the install to 0.2.0').
2. The commit-msg hook rejects it with a generic error that does not point at the offending char.
3. The skill offers no guidance that the exact version/proper-noun form can live in the commit body (which the hook does not validate).

## Acceptance Criteria

- conventional-commits/skill.yaml explicitly states the description charset (lowercase letters, digits, spaces, hyphens only) AND that exact version numbers/dots and proper-noun capitalization belong in the free-form commit body, not the subject; includes the Font Awesome and version-number examples.
- Guidance stays honest that this is stricter than the CC v1.0.0 spec (spec puts no charset limit on the description; body is free-form).
- commit-msg.py error output names the specific disallowed character(s) in the description.
- Catalog rebuilt; projected skill verified in sync (skills-check); commit-msg hook tests cover the char-naming; full suite green.
payload.title: conventional-commits skill omits the description charset rule the commit-msg hook enforces

## Context

Windows quality gate, run 33170058900 at fe96b60b (2026-08-28): `tests/test_runner_session_seed.py::test_a_pruned_seed_costs_a_re_read_and_not_the_round` fails with `FileNotFoundError: [WinError 2]` from `subprocess.Popen`. The test puts `stubcli` and `stubcli.cmd` on PATH; `runner.run` hands `argv` to `Popen` without a shell, and Windows `CreateProcess` resolves a bare name only to `.exe`, never through `PATHEXT` to `.cmd`. The same applies to the real `claude` binary on Windows, which npm installs as `claude.cmd`: the runner has never been able to spawn it from a bare name. `runner.py` uses `shutil.which` only for availability checks (lines 785, 976, 2159), not for the dispatch argv. Introduced with basicly-2kh170 (2a640140, 2026-08-27); the gate has been red on every run since.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On Windows: put `x.cmd` on PATH and run `subprocess.Popen(["x"])` - WinError 2. `subprocess.Popen([shutil.which("x")])` starts it.
2. `uv run pytest tests/test_runner_session_seed.py -k pruned_seed -q` on windows-latest.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN `runner.run` spawns a dispatch, IT SHALL resolve `argv[0]` with `shutil.which` before `Popen`, so a `.cmd` shim on Windows and a bare executable on POSIX both start, and IT SHALL report a command that resolves to nothing as a refused dispatch naming the command rather than raising `FileNotFoundError`.
- WHEN the resolved path is used, the recorded `command` on the run record SHALL still carry the spelling the spec declared, so ledger records stay comparable across machines.
- WHEN the regression test runs on any platform, IT SHALL put a `.cmd` twin and a bare shim on a temporary PATH and assert the dispatch starts through `runner.run`.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `tests/test_runner_session_seed.py`
- `changelog.d/<this-id>.fixed.md`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: the Windows job of `quality-gates` green on the landing commit, read from the job log.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the tier hook installer runs at project scope when it writes the settings command then the command contains no absolute interpreter path and no absolute repository path so the settings file stays committable and portable across machines and platforms, and given it runs at user scope then an absolute path is still written because that file is machine local, with tests that assert the project scope rendering carries neither
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

From the root of this repository, at the installer's default scope:

    python3 .basicly/core/kit/install_hook.py --host claude

Observed, written into `.claude/settings.json`, a tracked and committed file:

    "<redacted:posix-absolute-path><user><redacted:posix-absolute-path>" "<redacted:posix-absolute-path><user><redacted:posix-absolute-path>"

Both halves are machine and user specific. Expected: a command that a team can commit and that
resolves on every teammate's machine and on all three supported platforms.

The suite did not catch it because every test in `tests/test_kit_install.py` writes into `tmp_path`,
where the settings file is never a tracked file.

## Root cause

`hook_command()` in `.basicly/core/kit/install_hook.py` renders `sys.executable` and
`Path(hook_path).resolve()` unconditionally, for both scopes. Its docstring justifies this with "a
relative path would break the moment a spawn happened in a subdirectory", and
`test_the_written_command_names_the_hook_by_an_absolute_forward_slashed_path` asserts the rendering
with the same rationale, which turned the defect into a pinned requirement.

Verified 2026-08-01 against the live hooks documentation at code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks. That
rationale is CORRECT, and the counter argument recorded on this bead is WRONG. The docs say handlers
run in the current directory, not in the project root, and the current directory changes during a
session. This repository has already observed exactly that failure on 2026-07-26: a directory change
made its own relative path hook fail with `can't open file
'<repo><redacted:posix-absolute-path>'`. So a bare relative path is not the fix.

The documented fix is a placeholder that is neither absolute nor current directory dependent:
`${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` expands to the project root regardless of the working directory when the hook
runs. Present 18 times in the shipped 2.1.220 binary, against three positive controls and a negative
control that returned zero.

Interpreter, decided by the owner 2026-08-01 after the alternatives were measured: `uv run` rather
than a bare `python3`. Every committer to a basicly managed repo already needs uv on PATH because the
projected git hooks run `uv run python`, so for a basicly consumer this adds no dependency at all.
`--no-python-downloads` keeps the spawn path network free and makes it fail closed rather than
fetching an interpreter. Measured overhead about 117 ms, against a path far less frequent than the
Edit and Write hooks that already pay it. A bare `python3` was rejected because Windows ships no
`python3.exe` from the python.org installer and its App Execution Alias opens the Microsoft Store,
which is a worse failure than a clean one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the tier hook installer runs at project scope when it writes the settings command then the

payload.text:
FOUND 2026-08-01 by exercising the just-landed wbsz.3 installer against this repository rather than a scratch one - the failure only appears when the target settings file is TRACKED, which no test covered because every test writes into tmp_path.

MEASURED. Running python3 .basicly/core/kit/install_hook.py at the default project scope in this repo wrote this command into .claude/settings.json:

  "<redacted:posix-home-path>" "<redacted:posix-home-path>"

Both halves are machine specific and user specific. .claude/settings.json is a committed file here and in any consumer repo that shares agent configuration across a team, so the installer as shipped makes a repo uncommittable without leaking a username and a home directory layout, and the entry is broken for every teammate and every other machine. This repo forbids committing a machine or user specific absolute path outright, so the change was reverted rather than committed and this bead carries the fix.

The user scope case is NOT affected and must not be changed: ~/.claude/settings.json is machine local by definition, so an absolute path is the correct rendering there. The bug is scope specific.

WHAT MAKES THIS SUBTLE, and why the test suite passed. tests/test_kit_install.py has test_the_written_command_names_the_hook_by_an_absolute_forward_slashed_path which ASSERTS the absolute path, with the stated rationale that a relative path breaks the moment a spawn happens in a subdirectory. That rationale is an assumption I did not verify against the host docs and it is what locked the defect in. Check it properly before fixing: basicly's own managed claude hook already ships a RELATIVE command, uv run python .basicly/core/hooks/protect-generated.py, and has worked for many sessions, which is strong evidence that claude code runs hook commands from the project root and that a repo relative hook path is fine at project scope. Confirm against the live hooks documentation rather than against that inference, then invert the test.

THE HARDER HALF IS THE INTERPRETER, not the path. basicly's own hooks say uv run python, but the kit may not require uv - that is the whole point of the kit. A bare python3 is absent on many Windows installs where the launcher is py. Options to weigh: emit python3 with a documented Windows caveat; probe for an interpreter at install time and record the choice while still writing something relative; or ship a tiny launcher the host can invoke directly. Do not pick silently - the answer decides whether the kit is genuinely cross platform, and the repo targets Windows, Linux and macOS.

Filed P1 rather than P2 because the shipped default scope is the one every consumer gets first, and the failure mode is leaking a username into a commit.

Acceptance carried over:
## Trigger

When an agent-driven install deletes `.basicly` before running install, I want the guidance to say install over the top, or move `.basicly` aside and delete only after install succeeds, so I can avoid stranding the agent's own tooling mid-migration.

## Context

Reported by a consumer canary: an agent-driven install that deletes .basicly first breaks its own tooling mid-migration, because a Claude Code PostToolUse hook points at .basicly/core/hooks/tool-usage.py and every shell command fails the hook until install restores the tree. An install error at that point strands the agent with broken tooling and no obvious cause. The canary survived by moving the directory aside instead of deleting it. Guidance should say install over the top, or move aside and do not delete until install succeeds. This corrects advice this session gave a consumer.

payload.description:
## The finding

Reported by the lane that built the guard (basicly-vkh0.46), and left unfixed because it sits outside that record's acceptance criteria and its scope fence.

`write_snapshot` is now the single refusal point for a shrinking publish. It has three call sites. On the third, `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/fsck.py:736` in `fsck.rebuild`, the guard **cannot fire**: `rebuild` `unlink()`s every derived file before writing, so the target the guard would compare against is always absent, and the publish lands on the deliberate nothing-to-compare branch.

## Why it matters

`rebuild` is the path most likely to lose records, not least. The incident that bought R9 deleted 187 records, 47 of them open, and reported success. The lane reproduced that shape against `HEAD:snapshot.py`: a ledger whose log files vanish makes `rebuild` publish a 0-record snapshot over a 3-record one and return normally. The new guard refuses that when it is reached through the writer. Through `rebuild` it is still silent.

So the guard covers the paths that were already safest and not the one the requirement was written for. That is a fail-open shape: the gate exists, its tests are green, and the population it was bought to protect is outside its reach.

## The tension to settle, not a defect to patch blindly

`fsck`'s stated contract is delete and rebuild, never repair in place. The unlink is that contract, not an oversight. So this needs a decision, not an edit:

1. Have `rebuild` count the records of the file it is about to unlink, and pass that count as the comparison basis, keeping the unlink.
2. Have `rebuild` stop unlinking the snapshot and let `write_snapshot`'s atomic replace do the work, which makes the guard fire for free but changes fsck's contract.
3. Accept it, and record at the unlink why the guard is deliberately bypassed there.

Option 1 preserves both contracts and is the recommendation.

## Acceptance criteria

Given a rebuild whose source log has lost records, when it would publish a snapshot smaller than the one on disk, then it refuses and reports both counts, or it publishes and the reason the guard does not apply is stated at the call site.
Given the decision is taken, then a test drives the incident through `fsck.rebuild` and fails if the chosen behaviour regresses.
Given the guard's three call sites, then a test asserts which of them can reach the refusal and fails when a fourth is added without an answer.
Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_kit_tracker_fsck.py -k shrink -q

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/fsck.py`
- `tests/test_kit_tracker_fsck.py`

payload.description:
## Context

Owner, 2026-09-05: *"symbols on the board are not great (check what bootstrap icons have - it is fine to download that dependency and use it, do not use cdn and access online - web assets must be available without internet access)."*

## The constraint that shapes this

`tests/test_board_render.py` asserts the page carries no `<script`, no `<link` and no `src=`. The board is one self-contained HTML file a wall opens from disk. So an icon font, a stylesheet and a sprite URL are all refused by a gate that already exists.

That leaves **inline SVG paths**, which is also what this repo already decided for its own marks: `board_diagram` states that a mark is *"a `path` and never a codepoint, so it does not depend on a wall display font coverage"* - the owner reported tofu on a wall once already.

## What to vendor

`bootstrap-icons` as a dev dependency, its SVG sources committed under the kit rather than fetched. The build reads the handful of paths the page needs and inlines them; nothing at render time touches the network or the filesystem outside the repo.

## Acceptance Criteria

- THE PAGE SHALL still carry no `<script`, no `<link` and no `src=`, and SHALL still render with no network access.
- EACH icon SHALL be an inline `path`, never a codepoint, so a wall display font cannot tofu it.
- ONLY the icons the page draws SHALL be inlined; the full set SHALL NOT be embedded.
- THE VENDORED SOURCE SHALL be committed with its version and licence, and a test SHALL assert the inlined path matches the vendored file so a silent divergence fails.
- WHERE an icon replaces a drawn shape that already works, IT SHALL NOT be replaced without saying why.

## Scope

- `package.json`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/`
- `src/basicly/board_icons.py`
- `tests/test_board_icons.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- demonstration: open the board with the network down and read every mark

payload.description:
## Goal

Cut unnecessary complexity, dead code and ambiguous concepts out of basicly, and leave behind the deterministic and non-deterministic mechanisms that make a one-off pass unnecessary ever again.

## Why the mechanism half is not optional

**This analysis has already been run once.** `basicly-tcmy` is the 2026-08-01 architecture and code review: three read-only passes over the engine, the projector and the instruction catalog. Its own baseline reads *43 modules in a six-tier DAG*. Measured 2026-08-14: **86 modules, 42,966 lines**, and **13 of its children are still open**.

So a read-only pass that emits a prioritised list is a thing this repo can already produce. What it cannot do is **drain the list against feature pressure**. Commissioning a second audit without the draining mechanism buys a second backlog with the same fate, which is why pass 2 below is a precondition of the work being worth paying for rather than a follow-on.

The supporting measurement: `src/basicly/` went **36,641 to 42,966 lines in one week** with the module-size ratchet, the comment-density ratchet, the noqa ratchet, vulture, lint-imports and wired-or-deleted all live and green. **A ratchet bounds a file. Nothing bounds the tree.**

## The three passes

**Pass 0 - re-verify the inherited backlog.** Take `basicly-tcmy`'s 13 open children against today's tree and classify each done, moot, still-real or worse, with the check that decides it. A finding cites a `path:line` and code moves; an unverified inherited finding is a claim, not evidence. Adding new findings on top of an unverified backlog is how you get two backlogs.

**Pass 1 - the survey.** The `architect` role, at its declared maximum tier, over the tree. Output is a dependency-ordered backlog shaped so the plan gate admits it unchanged, so the loop can dispatch it without translation.

Scope exclusions, each with a reason rather than an exemption:

- `br.py` and the 32 `run_br` call sites across 12 modules - they leave the tree at the tracker flip (`basicly-u4xu`). Auditing a scheduled deletion spends budget the calendar already spends.
- `runner.py`'s subprocess dispatch path - replaced by `basicly-xjd2`.
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/` - no frozen surface, no declared schema, no cache decision. An audit needs a specification to judge against, and `work-tracker.md` section 7 now records that one does not exist.

**Pass 2 - the mechanisms.** Deterministic and non-deterministic, both, because each covers what the other cannot: a gate binds without judgement and cannot read intent; a role judges and cannot bind.

Non-deterministic, all already specified and none of them new inventions:

- `basicly-feje` - map `reviewer` to a phase so the per-lens adversarial review runs on every lane instead of never.
- `basicly-u2hl.22` - derive `change-shape` from an AST. This is the call-chain instrument; without it "a call chain that does not make sense" is a thing only a human notices.
- RETROSPECTIVE as a state with the special-cause trigger, so the system decides *when* a structural finding is worth acting on instead of tampering on every single occurrence.

Deterministic:

- `basicly-u2hl.27` - the controller and actuator. Set point, four sensors and the dampener already exist; what is missing is the thing that selects the next target and dispatches it. **This is the bead that decides whether any of the rest lands.**
- A tree-level size budget, because the per-file ratchets were all green through a 17%-in-one-week growth.
- `basicly-r343` - the dead-code gate reads English prose in a schema as a field reference, so it can pass a real finding.
- `basicly-plhx` - the agent schema lets a role ship with no tier, so D26's routing rule can be defeated silently.
- `basicly-a3yi` - resolve a declared tier into the projected surface, so a tier declaration reaches a spawn at all.

## Ranking rule for the backlog

Dependency order, not severity order. Severity decides what is in; dependency decides what is next. The finding that unblocks the most other findings goes first.

## Acceptance

- Given `basicly-tcmy`'s 13 open children, when pass 0 completes, then each carries a recorded verdict of done, moot, still-real or worse together with the command that decided it, and no finding is restated without re-verification.
- Given the survey scope and its three exclusions, when pass 1 completes, then every emitted item passes the plan gate unchanged and carries the measurement that found it.
- Given the emitted backlog, when it is ordered, then the order is by declared dependency and the graph is acyclic.
- Given pass 2, when it completes, then a controller selects and dispatches the next remediation target without a human choosing it, and a tree-level growth signal exists that the per-file ratchets cannot mask.
- Given this epic closes, when the next release boundary arrives, then the survey is re-runnable as a dispatch rather than reconstructed as a session.
payload.title: Architectural and design analysis, and the mechanism that retires it

payload.text:
[harness-info] the epic hid its own children for twenty minutes, 2026-08-14

Recorded because the trap is cheap to repeat and the symptom looks like nothing.

I wired this epic with five blocks-edges to the pass-2 mechanism beads that live in other epics: u2hl.27, feje, u2hl.22, r343 and a3yi. The intent was to say the epic cannot close until those land.

Effect: all 32 children became invisible to br ready. The ready set held 110 issues and not one of them was mine.

The discriminator was a comparison, not a theory. Three other open epics - tcmy, u2hl and jr0l - have 36 ready children between them, and every one of the three carries ZERO blocks-edges of its own. This epic carried five. Removing them took the ready set from 110 to 131 and surfaced 17 of the 28, which is exactly the number that carries no declared dependency.

Two probes were wrong before that one. My reimplementation of br's readiness rule gave 43 with parent-child counted as a blocker and 139 with it ignored; br reported 110, so neither model was right and neither could explain the absence. Do not diagnose this from the export.

The rule, stated so the next reader does not re-derive it: an epic used as a fan-out root declares no blockers. Record the dependency in the epic body instead. The five mechanism beads are named in the pass-2 section of this epic's description and they lose nothing by not being edges.

[harness-info] what the five surveys judged CLEAN, 2026-08-14

The 28 filed items are what the pass-1 surveys found. This is the other half: the modules they read and declined to file against, with the reason. Without it the next audit re-reads all of them from scratch and re-derives the same verdicts.

Every verdict below is one lane's judgment at `main` around 027e903. Treat it as evidence with a date, not as a permanent property.

## Essential complexity, deliberately not split

- `loop.py`, 29,816 tokens. Its sections are one responsibility: advance one track. The previous pass already cut `dispatch_brief`, `repair_brief` and `plan_entry` out of it, and the remaining seams are thin and coupled to `advance`. Splitting it now would be a metric-driven cut, which this repo's own rules forbid.
- `merge.py`, about 15,400 frozen tokens, 3.8 times the cap. No divergence found between its halves, and its attribution seam is deliberately the one both landing paths share. No split proposed.
- Marker parsing across `run_record.marker_payloads`, `decision_marker._marker_parts` and `artifact_record`. Three wire formats with three parsers, each cross-referencing the others and owning different header semantics. Unifying them would trade three simple parsers for one configurable one.
- `policy`'s grant, spend and marker-counter machinery. The additive-never-reset counters, the two-baseline grant metering and the refund bounds are one coherent invariant set that fragments badly if cut mid-family.
- Single-responsibility and left alone: `lane_log`, `working_set`, `landing_gate`, `rebase`, `checkout`, `contention`, `planner`, `state`, `dropin`, `catalog`, `scaffolds`, and the write half of `projection`. Several carry their own split provenance in the module docstring. `planner`'s containment reasoning is load-bearing security.

## Looks like a duplicate and is not

- `GRANT_COVERAGE` against `PROPOSAL_COVERAGE` in `policy`. Approval against origination, deliberately one level apart, documented at both sites.
- The two landing paths, `merge.merge_queue` and the supervisor's `route_outcomes`. They share their primitives through `merge.landing_order` and `merge.record_pass_couplings`, whose docstring names itself the one seam both go through. Composition, not reimplementation.
- `tuning.read_dispatches` against `run_record.dispatch_history`. Documented, with provenance as the stated reason, and the one behavioural difference argued in place. Watch, do not fix.
- `mirror.py`. Its only consumer is `br.py`, which is excluded. It is the dual-write mechanism the tracker flip activates, so it is pre-wired rather than dead.
- The per-target template files. They genuinely differ where they differ. Only the five-line `agents_md.j2` is byte-identical across families, and the renderer-shim question stays with `basicly-tcmy.21` and its Codex and Cursor counter-argument.

## Measured consolidated, no action

- **Token counting.** Exactly two `chars/4` sites repo-wide, `read_cost.py:74` and `runner_usage.py:88`. Both cite the design and `_text_tokens` carries its measured per-format error table.
- **Pricing a dispatch.** One site, `spend_calibration.calibrate_spend`, reached everywhere through the documented re-binding shim. One converter, `decompose.spend_from_working_set`.
- **Units at production.** Every producing site states its unit. The one genuinely dangerous pair, dollars against credits, already has separate fields and a warning comment.
- **Layering.** No undeclared upward import in any surveyed module. The only function-level imports carrying the `PLC0415` suppression are the two cycles `.importlinter` declares, and its alerting mode forces their removal when a cycle goes.
- **Constant-argument dead branches.** An abstract-syntax-tree scan over twelve modules re-found only the known `PassSpendAdmission.unforecast` and nothing else. The scan re-finding the known case is its positive control.
- **One name, one meaning.** `lane`, `pass` and `track` each carry exactly one meaning across the supervision layer. `model tier` against `capability tie

[harness-info] backlog state at 2026-08-15 close.

`e2mz.20` and `e2mz.21` closed. `.20` had landed and stayed open. `.21` closed with its
**premise refuted**: it asked for a gate asserting a fixture repo root is under `tmp_path`,
which would have passed while the damage happened, because `GIT_DIR` retargets git whatever
path a fixture passes - `e2mz.15` had established exactly that. The timing confirms a second
observation rather than a second defect: the nine fixture commits are 2026-08-14 19:51:21-42
and the scrub that fixes the class landed at 20:26:25. What shipped instead is the real gap
under it - an autouse `GIT_*` assertion in `tests/conftest.py`, binding the scrub over the
whole test population instead of the two sites `test_repo_isolation.py` names.

Two filed from measurement: `e2mz.23` (P0) and `e2mz.24`, both dual-write mirror defects,
both hit while closing the beads above.

**One finding cuts across the epic and is worth a gate of its own.** Five beads touched this
session named a demonstration check that selects **zero** tests, against positive controls
collecting 210, 142, 87 and 23 in the files they name. D18's plan gate refuses a field that
is absent or names nothing runnable; a backticked span matching nothing passes it. The
remedy is to run the criterion's own command and read the collected count. Recorded in
`factory-loop.md` §3.3 and in the plan's standing constraints.

payload.description:
## Context

Found by the `basicly-9rv0` lane 2026-08-14 while fixing the acceptance-heading predicate, and
deliberately left out of that lane's scope rather than widened into it.

`basicly-9rv0` established one definition of the acceptance heading in `plan_record` and made both
readers ask `plan_record.has_heading`. Three more sites still spell a plan-section heading
themselves, and each is the same drift risk one step weaker.

```text
supervise.py:1058     spells the acceptance heading as a dict key
decompose.py:1891     respells it, while using plan_record.SCOPE_HEADING and
                      plan_record.PLAN_HEADING in the same dict literal
policy.py:255         _SCOPE_SECTION = "## Scope", duplicating plan_record.SCOPE_HEADING
```

## Why this is weaker than the bug it came from, and still worth closing

The first two only **write** the heading, and they write it as a whole line, so neither can
currently disagree with the reader that parses it. `policy.py:255` is a second **definition** of a
literal `plan_record` already owns, which is the same shape `9rv0` just removed one instance of.

So the failure mode is not live today. It is that the next edit to any one of these four literals
has three silent twins, and this repository has paid for two-copies-that-disagree three times
already: `session_issue_ids` disagreed by 14 beads, and the context ceiling had two implementations
that reached opposite conclusions about a bead's fate.

## Headroom, measured before this bead was filed

`policy.py` carries 9 tokens of module-size headroom against its frozen baseline and 57.5 percent
prose against a 57.6 percent frozen share. `decompose.py` and `supervise.py` are both frozen too.
Removing a literal and importing the shared name is a net reduction in every one, so the ratchets
help rather than block here. Do not add explanatory prose to any of the three.

## Acceptance

- When a plan-section heading literal is searched for under `src/basicly/`, then exactly one
  definition of each exists and it lives in `plan_record`.
- When `supervise`, `decompose` and `policy` name a plan-section heading, then each reads it from
  `plan_record` rather than respelling it.
- When the change lands, then the module-size and comment-density figures for all three modules are
  at or below their frozen baselines.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `tests/test_plan_record.py`

## Demonstration

A test in `tests/test_plan_record.py` that asserts every plan-section heading literal reachable from
`src/basicly/` resolves to the `plan_record` constant, plus `uv run pytest -q` and
`uv run basicly verify --mode fast`.

payload.acceptance_criteria: When loader declares the fragment source vocabulary then it names one constant and the guard reads it with no inline set literal left at that site
payload.description:
## Context

Left as a residual by the `basicly-3oxp` lane 2026-08-14, which tripwired five of the six schema and
Python vocabulary pairs and could not reach the sixth without a source change outside its scope.

Two schemas declare the same two-value vocabulary:

```text
.basicly/core/schemas/fragment.schema.json   "source": {"enum": ["core", "user"]}
.basicly/core/schemas/agent.schema.json      "source": {"enum": ["core", "user"]}
src/basicly/loader.py:256                    if fragment.source not in {"core", "user"}:
```

The Python side is an **inline set literal inside a guard**, not a named constant, so there is nothing
for a tripwire to import and compare against. The pair is the only one of six that stays uncovered,
and the new module's docstring records the gap so it does not read as covered.

## Why the one-line change is the whole fix

Hoist the literal to a module constant - `SOURCES = frozenset({"core", "user"})` - and use it at that
guard. `tests/test_schema_vocabularies.py` then takes the pair as a sixth row in its `SCHEMA_ENUMS`
table and both mutation directions become checkable, exactly as the other five already are.

This is the same defect class the lane's own bead names and that this repository has now paid for
four times in one session: two declarations of one vocabulary that can drift apart silently. A
tripwire on five pairs and nothing on the sixth reads as covered, which is worse than no tripwire at
all.

## A second, differently shaped restatement the bead never named

All four schemas - `fragment`, `skill`, `agent` and `block` - declare
`"schema_version": {"const": 1}` against `schema.SOURCE_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1`. Same two-declaration
shape, but a **const rather than an enum**, so it needs a differently shaped row than `SCHEMA_ENUMS`
carries. Both halves belong in this bead because the fix is one table gaining two kinds of row.

## Acceptance

- When `loader` declares the fragment source vocabulary, then it names one constant and the guard
  reads it, with no inline set literal left at that site.
- When `tests/test_schema_vocabularies.py` runs, then the `source` pair is compared in both
  directions like the other five.
- When any of the four schemas restates `schema_version`, then a check compares it against
  `schema.SOURCE_SCHEMA_VERSION` and fails if they disagree.
- When a member is added to either side of any pair without the other, then the test fails - proven
  by mutation in both directions, with each probe reverted by hand.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loader.py`
- `tests/test_loader.py`
- `tests/test_schema_vocabularies.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_schema_vocabularies.py -q` passes with six enum rows and four
`schema_version` rows; then add `zzprobe` to one side of each new pair, read the failure, and revert
by hand. Paste both failures - a tripwire nobody has watched fail is a claim.

## Headroom, measured at main 866b821

`tests/test_schema_vocabularies.py` is new and well under the 4000-token cap. `loader.py` is not
frozen for size. Measure before writing prose anyway; a lane today lost that argument twice.

## Context

Left as residuals by the `basicly-967c` lane 2026-08-14. Both are confirmed-dead symbols the lane
proved with a probe and a positive control, and declined to delete because each is blocked by a file
outside its scope. Filing them so the verdicts are not re-derived.

## `loop_state.PHASES`

Confirmed dead in production. The only two `src/` references - `roles.py:66` and
`retrospective.py:42` - are **comments**. Live readers are all tests:

```text
tests/test_catalog_lint.py:536,547,557
tests/test_validate_gate.py:91,94
tests/test_retrospective.py:17,361
```

Blocked because `tests/test_catalog_lint.py` was owned by a concurrent lane and the other two are
tests of other modules. Note the standing warning that applies here: `PHASES` and
`config.LOOP_PHASES` differ by exactly one element, the terminal `done`, and the difference is
deliberate and documented at `config.py:369`. **Do not reconcile them** - the question is whether
`PHASES` has a reader, not whether the two agree.

## `loop_state.Ranking.fallback_sort`

Confirmed dead: declared at `loop_state.py:281,312`, and used only in constructors at
`tests/test_wip.py:240` and `tests/test_supervise.py:1082`. Positive control: the neighbouring
`fallback_rank` returns real production readers at `br.py:1029` and `supervise.py:2579`, so the probe
finds readers when they exist.

Blocked because it carries a `.scripts/wired_or_deleted.py` BASELINE entry at line 212. Deleting the
field without removing that entry turns the entry into a stale suppression and the gate red, and that
file was out of the lane's scope.

## The third item, and it is a scope defect rather than a symbol

`basicly-967c`'s acceptance criterion 3 - *"the six load-bearing entries each carry a note that it is
read within its own module"* - is **unreachable as that bead was dispatched**. Those notes live in
the `BASELINE` comments of `.scripts/wired_or_deleted.py`. The bead's own `## Scope` listed that file;
the dispatch brief removed it to avoid colliding with `basicly-kr7t`. So the criterion was dropped by
the dispatch, not by the work. It is carried here rather than left to look satisfied.

## Acceptance

- When `loop_state.PHASES` is searched for a production reader, then either one exists and is named,
  or the symbol and its tests are removed together and its suppression with them.
- When `Ranking.fallback_sort` is removed, then its `wired_or_deleted` BASELINE entry at line 212 goes
  with it in the same change, and the gate reports the same finding count as before.
- When the six load-bearing baseline entries are read, then each carries a note saying it is read
  within its own module.
- When the gate runs after the change, then it reports no new finding and no stale suppression.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop_state.py`
- `.scripts/wired_or_deleted.py`
- `tests/test_catalog_lint.py`
- `tests/test_validate_gate.py`
- `tests/test_retrospective.py`
- `tests/test_wip.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`
- `pyproject.toml`

## Dependency

Sequence this after `basicly-kr7t`, which extracts `.scripts/wired_or_deleted.py` and must not find
it changed underneath.

## Demonstration

`uv run python .scripts/wired_or_deleted.py` reports the same finding count as before with no stale
suppression, and `uv run pytest -q` green.

payload.acceptance_criteria: When a landing rebases a lane that changed a declared generated path then the path is rebuilt from the merged tree regardless of whether the rebase raised a conflict
payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-08-14 when lane `basicly-2j5a` bounced on `docs-claims` at its landing, hours after
`basicly-3w51` shipped the per-path rebuild that exists to prevent exactly that bounce.

The rebuild is triggered by a **rebase conflict**. Two lanes that each increment the same counter to
the same value produce **identical text**, so git auto-merges them cleanly, no conflict is raised, the
rebuild never fires, and the merged value is wrong by one.

Observed, not reasoned:

```text
base after basicly-3oxp landed          Test files | 163
lane basicly-2j5a's own block            Test files | 163   (correct in its pre-rebase tree)
after the rebase, no conflict raised     Test files | 163
the true value with both files present               164
```

The landing then failed on `docs-claims`, and regenerating in the rebased worktree produced 164.

## What worked and what did not, stated separately

**The gate failed safe.** `docs-claims` refused the landing rather than committing a false count, which
is the behaviour that matters most. Nothing wrong reached main.

**The mechanism did not do its job.** `basicly-3w51` exists so a lane does not bounce on a file it did
not author. Here the lane bounced anyway, and a human had to regenerate the block by hand and commit
it. That is the cost `3w51` was bought to remove, and it returns for every pair of lanes that move a
counter by the same amount - which for a counter incremented by one is the *common* case, not the rare
one.

## Why the conflict trigger is the wrong predicate

A conflict means the two sides disagree textually. What a generated block actually needs is a
rebuild whenever **its inputs changed**, and its inputs are the tree, not the file. Two lanes each
adding one test file change the input twice while writing the same text once.

So the predicate wants to be *the path is declared generated and this landing touched anything its
command reads*, or more simply: rebuild a declared generated path on every landing, unconditionally.
The command is deterministic and cheap - `docs_claims.py --fix --block` runs in well under a second -
so an unconditional rebuild costs almost nothing and removes a whole class of near-miss.

Note the tension to resolve rather than assume: `3w51` deliberately scoped the rebuild to conflicts
because the file is only **partly** generated and discarding both sides of the whole path would
destroy hand-authored prose. An unconditional rebuild must therefore stay block-scoped, which
`--block` already makes possible. That is why this is filed as a change to the trigger and not to the
resolution.

## Acceptance

- When a landing rebases a lane that changed a declared generated path, then the path is rebuilt from
  the merged tree regardless of whether the rebase raised a conflict.
- When two lanes each add one test file and land in sequence, then the second landing produces the
  true count without a human regenerating anything.
- When a rebuild runs, then hand-authored prose outside the marked block is unchanged, asserted
  against a lane that edited both.
- When the rebuild command fails or leaves a conflict marker, then the landing still bounces to the
  lane, as it does today.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/rebase.py`
- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `tests/test_rebase.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

## Warning

`tests/test_rebase.py` sits at exactly the 4000-token cap with zero headroom and is unfrozen -
`basicly-e2mz.2` is filed against precisely that. Sequence this after it, or expect the gate to refuse
the first line you add.

## Demonstration

Land two lanes that each add one test file, in sequence, with no human intervention between them, and
read the generated block on main: it must equal the tree. Then land a lane that edits the
hand-authored prose beside the block and confirm the edit survives.

payload.acceptance_criteria: When the two fields are compared then the population and time window each covers is stated and whether they are comparable at all
payload.description:
## Context

Surfaced 2026-08-14 by the board solution design and **verified by hand at main**:

```text
$ uv run basicly loop session basicly-kjc5 --json
token_budget     4,000,000
spent_tokens     177,970,761
```

44.5x over. Alongside it, over 357 dispatches: $953.82 spent, a $24.64 single-dispatch maximum,
1.25B tokens, and 12 `[harness-overrun]` markers.

## The figure is unclassified, and that is the whole bead

Two readings fit the same number and they call for opposite responses.

**Unenforced ceiling.** The grant spend halt did not fire for this root, and a control this repo
counts as working is not working. That is a P0.

**Scope mismatch.** `token_budget` is a per-grant figure while `spent_tokens` accumulates over every
grant the root has ever held, so the two are measuring different populations and the ratio is
meaningless. That is a reporting defect, and a smaller one.

The evidence points at the second without settling it: `stopped_bound` shows **9 `spend` firings** in
the run records, so the ceiling demonstrably does fire, and `factory-loop.md` section 15.7 keeps it as
a control on exactly that ground. But a control that fires nine times can still have a root it never
covers.

This is the same shape as two findings already recorded here: a band figure is not a spend figure,
and a delegated measurement can use the wrong unit. Re-derive the number against the unit the claim
is denominated in before calling it either thing.

## Why it gates other work

`basicly-rn0o.3` puts a spend panel on a wall display, and unwatched spend is the argument that
carries that whole project. **A board built over an unclassified number is observability over a
possibly-broken control.** Settle this first.

## Acceptance

- When the two fields are compared, then the population and the time window each covers is stated,
  and whether they are comparable at all.
- If they are not comparable, then either the reported pair changes so a reader cannot form a false
  ratio, or the surface states the window each covers.
- If the ceiling genuinely did not cover this root, then the gap is named with the code path that
  skips it, and this bead is re-filed as a P0.
- When the answer is recorded, then it names the command that produced it.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_policy.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly loop session basicly-kjc5 --json` prints a pair a reader cannot misread, and the
recorded answer names the command that settled it.

payload.acceptance_criteria: When requirement 10 is read then the original restatement and its reason are still present beside the amendment
payload.description:
## Context

Owner decision 2026-08-14, taken with the board solution design (`basicly-rn0o`).

`work-tracker.md` section 4.3 requirement 10 currently reads **restated** - *on-demand, not
real-time* - with the reason recorded at the site: *"A generated Mermaid/DOT graph and a static HTML
board rebuilt on write is not real-time, and calling it that would be the same overclaim one notch
smaller."*

The board's wall mode attaches to a live source. The owner re-opened the requirement **explicitly
rather than routing around it**, and the amendment is deliberately minimal.

## The amendment

Requirement 10 stays exactly as written. One sentence is added permitting a live-attached mode, under
two conditions that keep the original overclaim guard intact:

- it must display its own age, and
- it must never use the words "real time".

The first is enforced mechanically rather than by discipline: `harness-board/v1` makes `freshness` a
**required** top-level key, so there is no code path that renders a value without rendering its age.
That is why the amendment is safe - the guard moved from a word in a document into a schema.

## Why this is filed rather than just edited

The restatement is a recorded decision with an argument attached. Overwriting it silently is the
defect this repository keeps naming: a document that outlives the decision it records sends the next
reader to re-derive it. The amendment must land with its own reasoning beside the original, and the
original must stay legible.

## Acceptance

- When requirement 10 is read, then the original restatement and its reason are still present.
- When the amendment is read, then it names both conditions and points at the schema that enforces
  the first.
- When the words "real time" are searched for in any board-facing surface, then they do not appear as
  a claim about what the board delivers.

## Scope

- `docs/requirements/work-tracker.md`

## Demonstration

`rg -n 'real.time' docs/requirements/work-tracker.md` returns the amendment's prohibition and no
claim, and the section reads coherently to someone who has not seen this bead.

payload.description:
## Context

**The test suite corrupted the developer's real working repository on 2026-08-14.** Found when
`basicly worktree create` failed and `git status` began answering *"this operation must be run in a
work tree"*.

Three keys were written into `<redacted:posix-home-path>`, and a branch and a
worktree registration were created in the real repository:

```text
core.bare = true                              detached the entire working tree from git
user.name = Test
user.email = test@example.com
basicly.identityAllowEmail = @company\.com$    made every real commit fail identity-guard
branch harness/wt -> 15786c4                  a fixture commit, in the real repo
worktree registration -> <redacted:posix-absolute-path><redacted:machine-username><redacted:posix-absolute-path>
                          test_check_ignores_a_hook_edit0/repo.worktrees/wt
```

Timestamps place it inside one `pytest -q` run and exonerate the harness's own command:

```text
19:40:42   .git/worktrees/wt appeared
19:40:57   .git/config gained bare = true
19:41:18   basicly worktree create ran - the victim, not the cause
```

## Blast radius, and why it is a P0

Nothing was lost - all files were on disk throughout and `main` was intact - but for roughly one
minute the repository was unusable and **every gate in it was answering about the wrong tree**. A
developer who did not notice would have committed under a test identity, or been blocked by an
identity pattern no committed file declares.

It is also the sharpest possible violation of this repository's own rule that a fix must live in the
repo and never in the machine around it. Here the *tests* changed the machine around them.

## What is observed and what is hypothesis, kept apart

**Observed.** The leaked worktree path names `test_check_ignores_a_hook_edit_in_a_sibling_worktree`
(`tests/test_hooks.py:331`). At least seven test modules run `_git(repo, "config", "user.email",
"test@example.com")` - `test_verify.py:389`, `test_commit.py:581`, `test_checkout.py:29` among them.
The real repository gained a branch named `harness/wt`, which is the sibling-worktree naming those
tests use.

**Hypothesis, and it is the one that would make this a class rather than an incident.** A linked
worktree **shares `.git/config` with its parent repository**. So a test that creates a sibling
worktree and then runs `git config` against that worktree writes to the *shared* config - and if the
worktree was ever created against the real repository rather than a tmp fixture, the write lands
here. That would make every `_git(repo, "config", ...)` call in a worktree-creating test a loaded
gun, and it explains all three keys arriving together.

**Establish this before fixing it.** The wrong repair is to change the three call sites; the right one
depends on whether the fixture repo resolves correctly and the config write escapes anyway, or the
fixture repo itself resolved to the real root.

## Do not reproduce this carelessly

Running the full suite may corrupt the repository again. Reproduce inside a throwaway clone, and
snapshot `.git/config` before and after.

## Acceptance

- When the full suite runs to completion, then `.git/config` of the repository under test is
  byte-identical before and after, asserted by a test that reads it.
- When the suite runs, then no branch and no worktree registration exists in the real repository that
  the suite did not clean up.
- When a test needs a git identity or a config key, then it writes it to a fixture repository that
  cannot resolve to the developer's checkout, and a guard proves the resolution.
- Given the recorded incident, when the guard is applied to today's suite, then it names the site
  that produced it.

## Scope

- `tests/conftest.py`
- `tests/test_hooks.py`
- `tests/test_verify.py`
- `tests/test_commit.py`
- `tests/test_checkout.py`
- a new guard test

## Demonstration

Snapshot `.git/config`, the branch list and the worktree registry of a throwaway clone; run the full
suite; diff all three. All must be unchanged. Read the diff, do not assert it.
